terms.definition: A structured collection of values arranged along one or more axes, typically with a common data type. Its shape and type govern which numerical operations are valid and how results should be interpreted.
A tuple describing the length of an array along each axis. For example, `(3, 4)` identifies three rows and four columns, for 12 elements total.
The number of axes in an array. A one-dimensional vector has one axis, while a table-like array commonly has two. Dimension count alone does not explain what each axis represents.
An operation that changes an array's arrangement while preserving its values and total element count. A reshape is only possible when the products of the old and new dimensions match.
An operation applied separately to corresponding array elements, such as adding values in matching positions. It differs from matrix multiplication, which combines values across an axis.

A plot that groups values of one numeric variable into bins and displays a count or other summary for each bin. Its visual shape depends on the binning rule and does not retain pairings with other variables.
A plot that places paired numeric observations at horizontal and vertical coordinates. It helps inspect patterns such as clustering or curvature, but does not by itself prove causation.

A plotting backend that produces image files without requiring a graphical desktop or opening an interactive window. It is useful in servers and automated jobs, but rendered output still needs visual review.
A numeric value that is not finite, such as NaN or positive or negative infinity. Such values may invalidate summaries or plots and should be handled with an explicit, reported rule.

The ability to rerun an analysis with documented inputs, code, and dependencies and obtain traceable results. Reproducibility supports verification, but does not guarantee that assumptions or interpretations are correct.
